utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. With that, I have concluded the housekeeping matters that I wanted to bring to Your Honours' attention, and I will begin my remarks. Let me begin, Your Honours, by publicly acknowledging and expressing my gratitude for the thorough manner in which the Trial Chamber has proceeded in this case. Both the psychological report prepared by Ana Najman, specialist in clinical psychology, and the report on the comparative analysis of sentencing practices that was prepared by Dr. Ulrich Sieber of the Max Planck Institute were of considerable assistance to me in this case. This is a very important case for the Tribunal, and I concede it is a very difficult case. Mr. Deronjic is guilty of a terrible crime. He has also provided invaluable evidence about a broad range of issues that will enable the Office of the Prosecutor to fulfil its mandate to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. Thus, it is a case that creates a considerable tension between determining the proper punishment for someone who is responsible for the gravest of crimes, yet someone who has also taken significant and substantial positive steps to assist the Prosecutor. Your task is to find the right balance between punishing the perpetrator for the commission of a serious crime, while at the same time not discouraging other persons similarly situated to the defendant from cooperating with and providing valuable assistance to the Prosecutor in the future. For my part, I have approached this issue carefully, having consulted with the Prosecutor and with my colleagues, and having considered the purposes and objectives of this Tribunal. The mandate given to the Office of the Prosecutor is to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. To do that, it is necessary to unravel facts about events that quite often states and individuals are unwilling or reluctant to yield, but without which the Office of the Prosecutor cannot proceed. We have been engaged in this effort for a decade. In the final analysis, the ability of my office to prosecute individuals for the commission of serious crimes in the former Yugoslavia depends on our ability to obtain evidence. For my part, after careful consideration of all of the imperatives that go into the process of investigating and prosecuting effectively the complex crimes that fall within our mandate, after cogitating on what are the purposes to be served by sentencing and what is an appropriate punishment for someone who is guilty of a significant crime, understanding that our mandate includes ascertaining the truth about the specific crime being prosecuted, in this case, Glogova, as well as other crimes that are being investigated and prosecuted by my office, understanding the importance and the need to gain a better understanding of other crimes and persons responsible for the commission of those crimes, and finally, after a careful assessment of the degree of cooperation of the accused, I and other members of my office came to a judgement about what sentence the Office of the Prosecutor would recommend to Your Honours. It was not an easy decision, and one that may frustrate and anger some, but it was a decision that was made in good faith and with careful attention to ensuring the ability of my Office to fulfil its broad mandate. Let me begin with a review of the case history. On the 6th of July 2002, Miroslav Deronjic was arrested on a sealed indictment dealing with the crimes that occurred in Glogova. On the 10th of July 2002, the defendant made his initial appearance on those charges. Approximately 14 and a half months later, on the 30th of September 2003, and well before a trial date was selected, Miroslav Deronjic entered a plea of guilty to the charge of persecutions contained in the second amended indictment. The charge of persecutions related to the attack on the village of Glogova. And it is for those acts and those acts alone that Mr. Deronjic is before you today. His guilty plea was the result of a plea agreement that was filed with the Trial Chamber and is a matter of public record. By its terms, the plea agreement identifies the maximum term that the Trial Chamber could impose for his guilty plea, a term of imprisonment up to and including the remainder of his life. The plea agreement states in paragraph 11, subpart A, that based on Miroslav Deronjic's full and substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor will recommend to the Trial Chamber that it impose a term of ten years' imprisonment. The plea agreement further states in clear and explicit terms that the Trial Chamber is not bound to accept the Prosecutor's recommendation and may impose a sentence above or below the Prosecutor's recommended sentence. Now, in thinking about the nature of this crime, I reflected on the background of the origin of this institution, which I think bears repeating here. Following reports of serious violations of international humanitarian law occurring in the former Yugoslavia, the UN commissioned an impartial commission of experts to analyse the situation in the former Yugoslavia. The interim report of the commission of experts was filed with the UN Security Council in February of 1993. Based on the contents of that report, the UN Security Council passed Resolution 808 in which it expressed "its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring within the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including reports of mass killings, and the continuance of the practice of ethnic cleansing." The Security Council determined that this situation constituted a threat to international peace and security, and on the 25th of May 1993, passed Resolution 827 by which it established this Tribunal. In doing so, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Security Council was convinced that the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law would contribute to the restoration and maintenance of peace. The establishment of the truth by this Tribunal is a vital component to the effort to restore and maintain peace in the former Yugoslavia. As stated in the Erdemovic judgement, and I quote: "The discovery of truth is a fundamental step on the way to reconciliation." Now, let me turn to the gravity of the crime that was committed in Glogova on the 9th of May 1992. Much of what I am going to say is already expressed in the factual basis that's a matter of public record. The crime for which Miroslav Deronjic is to be sentenced is precisely the type of crime about which the Security Council expressed its grave alarm in Resolution 808. The events in Glogova on the 9th of May 1992 are a classical case of ethnic cleansing, and precisely the reason why the Security Council established this Tribunal. The attack on Glogova was not an isolated or random event, but a critical element in a larger scheme to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina and create Serb-ethnic territories. Vital to this scheme to create Serb-ethnic territories was the separation and permanent removal of non-Serb populations from municipalities designated as Serbian. The Bosnian Serb leadership intended that the creation of Serbian-ethnic territories would be created either by agreement or by force. Mr. Deronjic, who was the highest-ranking Bosnian Serb official in the Municipality of Bratunac subscribed unequivocally to the policy of creating Serb-ethnic territories within Bosnia and to the policy of using force to remove Muslims from the territory. To achieve this objective, military, police, and paramilitary forces from within Bosnia, and from Serbia, were utilised. On the 17th of April, 1992, volunteers from Serbia entered Bratunac and issued an ultimatum to the Bosnian Muslims in Bratunac to surrender their weapons and legal authority to the Bosnian Serbs where they would be destroyed. The Bosniaks acquiesced to this demand. Thereafter, efforts to ethnically cleanse the Muslims from the Bratunac Municipality were undertaken. Bosnian Muslim villages were disarmed, including the village of Glogova that is the subject of the indictment before you. Glogova was a village in the Bratunac Municipality, and I have submitted to Your Honours a copy of a map. I don't have the exhibit number yet on it, but it should be the next in order. And if I could have the assistance of the usher, we could put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit PS21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is -- this map shows the location of Glogova, and in relation particularly to the town of Bratunac. According to the 1991 census, Glogova had a population of 1.913, 1.901 of whom were Bosniaks. In late April of 1992, the JNA unit arrived in Bratunac. It participated in the efforts to disarm the Muslim villages. On the 5th of January -- I'm sorry, on the 5th of April 1992, a decision to attack Glogova was made. The participants in the attack were members of the local TO, Territorial Defence; the JNA;, and "volunteers," all of whom acted in unison to achieve their common goal. At a crisis staff meeting on the night before the attack presided over by Miroslav Deronjic, he explained that the plan to create Serbian ethnic territory could not be implemented in the Bratunac Municipality without taking Glogova and transferring the entire Muslim population from Bratunac. The intent to attack was to transfer the entire Muslim population of Glogova to non-Serb territory. In other words, the plan was to ethnically cleanse the Muslims from Glogova. Mr. Deronjic knew that the attack on Glogova was part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against the Muslim civilian population within Bosnia, and that the attack was done to further a plan to create Serbian ethnic territories within Bosnia. On the 9th of May 1992, in the early morning hours, Glogova was attacked, and there was no resistance from the Muslim residents of the village. Mr. Deronjic was personally present, and his participation in this attack is described in the factual basis. During the attack, a substantial number of Muslim houses were burned to the ground. Mr. Deronjic authorised some of those houses be burned. 65 Muslims civilians were murdered. Mr. Deronjic did not kill any of them personally, but at the time he ordered the attack on the village, it was foreseeable to him and he was prepared to take the risk that innocent civilians would be murdered. All of the Muslim residents of the village were expelled from the municipality of Bratunac. The attack on Glogova was a perfectly executed act of ethnic cleansing directed at a village that had been disarmed. The cleansing of the village and the attacks on other Muslim settlements that followed was intended to contribute to the larger plan of creating Serbian ethnic territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is our submission to Your Honours that there are two factors which aggravate this crime and should be considered by the Trial Chamber, the superior position held by the accused and the vulnerable and helpless population of Glogova, it having been disarmed well before the attack and having offered no resistance during the attack. It is beyond dispute that the crime for which Mr. Deronjic has been convicted is extremely grave. And that is certainly the most important factor to be considered in determining sentence. We have included in our submissions the statements of a number of victims from the tragic events from the 9th of May 1992. The unimaginable horrors and the enduring consequences of this attack suffered by the victims are described in our submissions. They reflect the impact this crime had on the lives of the former residents of the Glogova community, and they reflect, among other things, the destruction of an entire Muslim community. Victims who suffered the loss of numerous family members, one of the victims reports losing 14 members of her extended family; another, 9 members. These submissions of ours reflect the victims who suffered the loss of their homes and all of their material possessions, victims who lost the ability to earn a livelihood, victims who described being wrenched from a peaceful prosperous life where there was no want, to a life of bleakness and despair in refugee camps, victims who describe traumatic long-term effects such as continual nightmares, or serious traumatic effects on the child victims. The nature of the crime and the indescribable suffering of the victims stemming from the acts for which the accused bears responsibility and to which he has admitted merits the severest of sentences. Without substantial mitigation, I would have had no hesitation in asking you to impose such a sentence. This is, however, an unusual case where substantial mitigating factors exist. These substantial mitigating factors, in my respectful submission, warrant the imposition of a sentence of a lesser magnitude. Because I will be asking the Trial Chamber to accept a sentence recommended in the plea agreement, a sentence of ten years' imprisonment, it is my responsibility to inform you and to inform the public why I am making this recommendation. The first factor in mitigation is Mr. Deronjic's early plea of guilty and his acceptance of responsibility for the crimes which he authored. In the factual basis, Mr. Deronjic details the events leading up to the commission of the crime, his role in it, as well as the role of other individuals and entities; paramilitaries, the JNA, the Territorial Defence. I'll describe this later in my remarks. The jurisprudence of the ICTY has recognised that an early guilty plea is a mitigating factor for three reasons: One, it obviates the need for victims to give evidence and saves considerable time and resource of this ad hoc Tribunal; two, it is important in establishing the truth about what happened; and three, it is a fundamental step in contributing to reconciliation. For all of these reasons, it is our respectful submission to Your Honours that Mr. Deronjic should be given credit for his early plea of guilty. Now, Rule 101(B)(ii), of the Tribunal's Rules of Evidence and Procedure expressly provides that "the Trial Chamber shall take into consideration the substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. convicted person before or after conviction." According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, substantial cooperation depends on the extent and quality of the information provided by the accused, and can include the prior giving of evidence on behalf of the Prosecution, the provision of new information replete with identities and names of perpetrators, substantiation and corroboration of existing information, and future cooperation, including testifying on behalf of the Prosecution. In our judgement, the cooperation provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Miroslav Deronjic has been substantial within the meaning and the intent of this Rule. Let me draw a comparison to a case that I'm quite familiar with, the case of Drazen Erdemovic. I was involved, as I mentioned earlier, in that investigation, in that indictment, in that prosecution. I was not involved in the second plea of guilty by Mr. Erdemovic. Mr. Erdemovic entered a guilty plea in his second plea of guilty to the charge of a violation of the laws or customs of war for his participation in a mass execution that occurred on the 16th of July 1995 at the Branjevo Military Farm. Following a successful appeal, he entered a guilty plea for the second time, and he received a sentence of five years, in part because of the unique element of duress that existed in his case, and in part because of his substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor. As I recall, Judge Mumba was the President of the Trial Chamber in that case. I can say this many years after that plea that Mr. Erdemovic's cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor was significant then, and his continuing cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor is significant now. Now, what was his cooperation? In brief, I will describe it. He confirmed that an execution took place at the Branjevo Military Farm on July the 16th 1995 and he described his role in it. He identified the location of another mass execution, a very short distance away, the Pilica cultural dom, a location about which we had no information. He identified perpetrators who were responsible for the executions at the Branjevo Military Farm and at the Pilica cultural dom, and he testified in the Rule 61 hearing against Karadzic and Mladic - I participated in that myself and led his evidence - and he testified in the Krstic case; I led his evidence in that case. He testified in other cases as well. Mr. Erdemovic provided unique and important evidence and insight into one event, the massacres at Srebrenica in 1995. The information and evidence provided by Mr. Deronjic to the Office of the Prosecutor is vastly broader, both in terms of the subject matter, and in terms of the time covered by the events he describes, from 1991 to 1995. It is precisely because of the level and the extent of Mr. Deronjic's cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor that my office has made its sentencing recommendations to Your Honours. For your benefit and for the benefit of the public, I will outline the form and substance of his cooperation with my office. Starting with the information that he has provided to my office, we took an extensive statement from Mr. Deronjic about a wide-ranging number of topics relating to events in Bosnia from 1991 to 1995. It is very significant to note that at the time Mr. Deronjic provided these statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, he did so without any promises of reward or benefit. This certainly warrants your consideration. Now, we have filed a copy or there is filed with this Chamber, I believe it is DS8, a copy of his statement that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. I do not intend to go into great detail about all of the information provided by Mr. Deronjic in this statement. It's 71 pages long, and it speaks for itself. It's a matter of public record. Nevertheless, I will touch upon some of the information that he provided to you so that you and the public are aware of the extent of his cooperation with my office. I will start with the information that he provided to us about the organisation of the Bosnian Serb leadership in 1991 and 1992. In his extensive statement, Mr. Deronjic describes the political philosophy that animated the Bosnian Serb leadership following the Bosnian Assembly decision in October of 1991 to support the creation of a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. A central principle of the Bosnian Serb leaders was the creation of Serbian ethnic territories and the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This included the separation and permanent removal of ethnic populations from municipalities designated as Serbian, either by agreement or by force. In respect of the indictment that is before you, this political agenda culminated in 1992 in the Bratunac Municipality with the ethnic cleansing of Glogova and adjacent villages. Turning my attention to a second piece of information that Mr. Deronjic has expounded on, the variant A and variant B document. One significant step in the prewar efforts of the Bosnian Serbs to establish control in selected municipalities is reflected in this document that was disseminated to the Bosnian Serbs by Radovan Karadzic on the 19th of December 1991. The document we have referred to in the course of our hearing yesterday was known as the variant A and variant B document, Mr. Deronjic provided testimony to you yesterday and answered your questions about this particular document, its creation, who was present at the meeting, and the like. My next exhibit - we don't have to put it on the ELMO but I do need a number for it - is a copy of the variant A and variant B document. If we can get that number, then I can identify it move on.
