utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, there's no need to repeat to what Mr. Deronjic said about variant A and variant B. It's in his testimony and it is in his statement. I do know that the authenticity and the admissibility of this particular document was vigorously disputed in two trials before this Tribunal, the Prosecutor versus Simic et al, and the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin. It is my submission that had his testimony been available both in Simic and Brdjanin cases, it would have been of considerable assistance to the Trial Chambers that heard those cases. I can say unequivocally to Your Honours that his testimony on this subject will be of assistance to the Prosecutor in future trials, and in particular, the Krajisnik trial that is coming up, due to start on the 3rd of February. Now, Mr. Deronjic also has provided us with information, and considerable information, about another prewar element in the takeover of the Bratunac Municipality and the adjacent municipalities, the arming of the Bosnian Serbs. He provided unique information about his trip to Belgrade with the late Goran Zekic and his contact with Mihajlo Kertes, the assistant SFRY minister of the interior about the supply of arms to Bosnia. In that context, and in respect of Bosnia, he quotes Kertes as saying: "In the area of 50 kilometres from the Drina River, everything would be fully Serbian." This statement was made well before the strategic objectives that Your Honours have before you, well before those objectives were promulgated by the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May 1992. He also provided information to the Office of the Prosecutor how arms were provided by the Bosnian Serbs in the Podrinje region, how they were provided by the SFRY, where these arms came from, how they were delivered to Bosnia, to whom they were delivered, where they were stored. In addition, he informed us about other channels by which the Bosnian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs in the region were provided with arms. In other prosecutions that are pending before this Tribunal, this evidence will be quite important, and his evidence has been of considerable assistance to us. Let me focus on another topic about which Mr. Deronjic gave us information, and that is the takeover of Bratunac Municipality on the 17th of April 1992. The information that he provided to us was both unique and corroborative of information already in the possession of my office. Central to the takeover of Bratunac on this date was the role of the volunteers. Mr. Deronjic provided us with unique insight into who those volunteers were, where they came from, and what role they had in the takeover itself. The events that occurred in Bratunac are an element and an important element in an indictment that is pending against Mr. Krajisnik, whose trial will start next week. Mr. Deronjic also gave us insight into and described a pattern of conduct in Bosnian Serb takeovers in various municipalities. He described that pattern to us. He described how volunteers and the JNA worked in conjunction with local Serbs to take over power in other municipalities in order to create Serb-ethnic territories. This is very important evidence to the Office of the Prosecutor. In respect of the takeover of Bratunac, he provided a detailed account on the arrival of the JNA unit to the Bratunac Municipality, identifying that unit and its commander, and describing the significant role that that JNA unit had in the disarming of Bosnian Muslims and in ethnically cleansing the municipality of those people. Much of the information that Mr. Deronjic provided to us is unique and will be significant in other prosecutions. Turning to the takeover of Glogova itself, in the factual basis and his testimony before you yesterday, he described the events leading up to the takeover of the village. Those are set forth as well in the factual basis, in paragraphs 14 through 37. Mr. Deronjic's description of the events leading up to the attack and his insights and reasons for the attack and how the attack fit into the overall plan to create Serb-ethnic territories have been invaluable to the Office of the Prosecutor and will be invaluable to others who must make judgements both legal and historical about the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Deronjic provided details about the actual attack on Glogova. Those are set forth in paragraphs 38 through 43 of the factual basis, and he related additional details yesterday in his testimony before you. I can say that the information that he has provided to us is both unique and corroborative. He has provided information as to the identities of perpetrators, and he has provided information to us that is corroborative of those events that we already knew. Finally, in respect of the attack on Glogova, Mr. Deronjic described both in paragraphs 45 through 47 of the factual basis and in his testimony yesterday an important meeting that he attended in Pale immediately after the attack where he reported to Ratko Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, and Velibor Ostojic, and to the heads of other municipalities about the events in Glogova. He informed us how he was applauded for that report and how Velibor Ostojic said: "Now we can colour Bratunac blue." This is significant and important information to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Deronjic also provided information about the forcible removal and transfer of Bosnian Muslims from the Bratunac Municipality in April and May of 1992. While the manner in which this ethnic cleansing took place was already known to the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Deronjic's accounts were valuable because they corroborated our earlier evidence. His detailed evidence regarding the events leading up to the attack, the purpose of the attack, and his ability to put it into context, into a greater plan, will be important evidence in a number of future cases. Let me turn to another topic about which Mr. Deronjic has provided the Office of the Prosecutor valuable information, and that is the presence of Red Berets in Bratunac between 1992 and 1993. Mr. Deronjic described for us the presence of Red Beret training camps in the Bratunac Municipality and in adjacent municipalities. I am informed and can report to Your Honours that other prosecutors in other cases find this evidence unique, valuable, and will be presenting it in other matters, in other cases pending before this institution. One of the important issues to this Tribunal and to historians is whether the Yugoslav Army participated in combat activities within Bosnia after the JNA moved out of Bosnia. That has been a matter of debate and contention as long as I have been in this institution. In April of 1993, a Serb counteroffensive against Bosnian Muslim forces occurred in the Bratunac area. At this point in time, the Yugoslav Army was supposed to be out of Bosnia. They were not. Mr. Deronjic personally observed and identified units of the JNA that were present in the Bratunac area engaged in combat. He testified about this and other matters in the Milosevic case. The assessment of his evidence in the Milosevic case by Mr. Geoffrey Nice who was the lead Prosecutor in that case was that his evidence was helpful. Mr. Deronjic provided us information about Srebrenica in 1995. He provided us information about the mass killings that occurred, and his information was both unique and corroborative. It included the following: Information about his meetings and contacts with Radovan Karadzic before, during, and after the tragic events of Srebrenica. The information that he provided to us was clearly helpful to a future prosecution; it was unique; and in many respects, it has been corroborated. He provided unique information about the role of Colonel Ljubisa Beara in the mass executions. Colonel Beara was a central figure in this murderous scheme, and he has been indicted by this Tribunal for his role in the mass killings. He is currently a fugitive. Mr. Deronjic's testimony in that case will be quite important. Mr. Deronjic has acknowledged that mass executions in Srebrenica occurred. This is important. I was involved, as I mentioned yesterday, in the Srebrenica case since the OTP commenced its investigations in July of 1995. I travelled to the various execution sites personally. I've travelled to Glogova where there was a mass grave. I've had -- I witnessed first-hand the reluctance of people in the Republika Srpska to talk about these events, let alone acknowledge them. I summoned and spoke to countless Republika Srpska military officers and personnel, all of whom refused to acknowledge that any massacres occurred. I prosecuted General Krstic for 15 months for his responsibility in those events. It was clear to me then and it is clear to me now that acknowledging these massacres occurred remains very difficult for many people in the Republika Srpska and remains a significant impediment to reconciliation. This stubborn insistence that nothing illegal happened in Srebrenica in the face of overwhelming and irrefutable evidence to the contrary is truly amazing. Slowly, however, this is changing, particularly as a result of the efforts of this institution. I refer to the Krstic case where detailed forensic evidence and witness accounts exposed the truth, and to the ongoing trial of Blagojevic and Jokic. I also refer to the guilty pleas of Dragan Obrenovic and Momir Nikolic where they acknowledge their roles in the killings. Their public acknowledgments that the massacres occurred has contributed to the process of reconciliation by acknowledging the truth about those events. Surely, Mr. Deronjic's public acknowledgment and information that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor about those same events can only contribute to the process of establishing the truth and advancing reconciliation. Why do I raise this? I say this because in the Republika Srpska, there is still a considerable effort to deny these events at Srebrenica. The revisionists are still hard at work. My next exhibit I will use, if I could have a number for it, is a report. If I could have a number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we attach a number, may I please hear the Defence on this and the relevance of this document for this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to provide some additional information because as you correctly stated beforehand, this Trial Chamber is seized, and we emphasised this already yesterday, is seized only with the events the 9th of May 1992 in Glogova. We acknowledge that the Prosecution by tendering this document and the now-following documents related to Srebrenica want to show how important it is for the people in the area to know that not the propaganda in the area is the truth, but participants themselves here contributed in finding the truth. And for this reason, it might not be necessary to tender this into evidence. This might confuse the assessment in public of what is our case. And therefore if you really believe it's necessary to tender, could you please elaborate on the relevance, the added relevance of these documents for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to, Mr. President and Your Honours. This document, what we're talking about is the contribution of Mr. Deronjic to the Office of the Prosecutor and the ramifications of that cooperation. Mr. Deronjic has given us a significant statement in which he has provided details about Srebrenica and about persons' roles in it, about the fact that massacres occurred, about a document that he prepared, which I will get to, I hope to, in a few minutes, all of which tends to fuel the revisionists' ability to distort what happened. And if there is credit due to Mr. Deronjic and others who acknowledge that crimes took place, it is for the purpose of, one, establishing the truth; and two, undercutting the ability of future revisionists to distort historically what happened. As long as the revisionists are able to continue with these wild distortions, and they don't hear from people like Mr. Deronjic or Mr. Obrenovic or Mr. Nikolic, then they will have the field to themselves, and they will contribute significantly. If those voices are muted, there will be significant license for the revisionists to continue to block reconciliation. So the reason I am raising this document is to give you a concrete illustration of revisionist -- revisionism at its worst. This document was prepared in 2002. So that is the purpose of my raising this, because I think it's an appropriate consideration for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, the Trial Chamber will convene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document called "Report on case Srebrenica, the first part," is hereby admitted into evidence. May we hear the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered Exhibit PS23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This document, PS23 which I will not put on the ELMO, but I will put a portion on the ELMO, was prepared -- is entitled "documentation" -- I'm sorry -- was prepared by the documentation centre of the Republika Srpska Bureau of Government of RS for Relation with ICTY. It was prepared in September of 2002. The avowed purpose of this report is as follows, and I quote from the introduction: "The goal of this report is to present the whole truth about crimes committed in Srebrenica region regardless of the nationality of perpetrators of crimes and time when they were committed." Now, on the ELMO at page 34 of this report, and throughout this report it refers to the "alleged Srebrenica massacres," it concludes on page 34, and in the top paragraph that "the number of Muslim soldiers who were executed by Bosnian Serb forces for personal revenge or for simple ignorance of international law would probably stand less than 100." This document is obscene, and it is historical revisionism at its worst. Mr. Deronjic's acknowledgment that the massacres occurred and his information that he provided us about the roles of individuals in those massacres will contribute to the vile distortions of the truth that continue to circulate in the Republika Srpska. Now, while I'm speaking about this report, another canard that is found within this report is the suggestion that Bosnian women, children, and the elderly were humanely transferred from the enclave. The contrary of that has been demonstrated time and time again through the testimonies of many witnesses who have appeared before this Tribunal in both the Krstic case, and in the Blagojevic and Jokic trials. Information provided by Mr. Deronjic confirms that what occurred was a forceful -- forcible displacement of the Muslim population. And let me turn to the next exhibit, if I can, and if I could have a number for that, it is a declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit PS24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could put that on the ELMO as well. This is a document with which I am quite familiar. It was an exhibit in the Krstic case. I'm certain that it's an exhibit in the Jokic and Blagojevic cases. It is a document that has helped fuel the idea that the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica were humanely transferred from Srebrenica. This is a document that was signed by Mr. Deronjic, by Mr. Nesib Mandzic, who was a Muslim representative of the population in Potocari at the time, and by Major Franken, who was a Dutch battalion deputy commander at the time. And what this document says, in the operative phrases, is that the Muslims in Srebrenica had a choice of remaining in the enclave or being evacuated. If they wanted to be evacuated, they had a choice as to the direction they would be evacuated, that the evacuated would be carried out by the Bosnian Serb Army and police, supervised and escorted by UNPROFOR. And finally, that the Serbs carried out the evacuation in accordance with international humanitarian law. Now, this document has been central in the efforts to continue with that fictitious story. And I have four exhibits, if we could have those numbered next, I will run through them very quickly and in succession.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first exhibit, on the top region east Europe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There should be numbers on the upper right-hand corner that will assist you in identifying them. 114/1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Exhibit PS25 for the B/C/S original and 25A for the translation. The next exhibit, 114/2, PS25/1. Next exhibit, OTP Exhibit 113/3 in the upper right corner is PS25/2. And last exhibit numbered OTP Exhibit 114/4 in the upper right corner will be PS25/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we have to come back to this because at least in my collection, we sometimes have only the B/C/S or the English version, but not both of them. But we accept this and admit these documents into evidence in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These documents, Your Honour, are reflections of the proposition that nothing happened in Srebrenica, and they are exhibits that show that this deception started as early as the 17th of July 1995. If we could have the first of those exhibits put on. What is the number in the upper right-hand corner of that exhibit? This is -- I'm used to it as 114/1. It's PS25, I believe. And in this document, which is a summary, it discusses how Mr. Zametica, who was the spokesperson for Mr. Karadzic, says that the description of what happened in Srebrenica by the international media is violent propaganda unrealistically reporting on the events relating to the situation in Srebrenica. If we turn to the next exhibit, which is 114/2 on the upper right-hand corner, this is also a report, 17th of July 1995, talking about a -- from Mr. Zametica. And it says: "Talk of the Muslims being expelled is totally false, as confirmed by the fact that the evacuation was prearranged with representatives of Muslims civil authorities." If we turn to the next exhibit, which is -- it was previously Exhibit 114/3, Mr. Zametica continued with his denials, and indeed he says that "the evacuations were conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions," as reflected in the previous document that I showed you, the document that was prepared by Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Franken, and Mr. Mandzic, and Mr. Deronjic is indeed even mentioned in this news summary of the 18th of July. And finally, if we turn to the last of these four exhibits, we will see Mr. Karadzic on the 5th of November 1995 saying that nothing happened in Srebrenica. I only point this out to show Your Honours that this fearsome effort to distort the truth continues in the Republika Srpska. It started while the killings were taking place, and it continues through official reports emanating from the Republika Srpska in 2002. This particular exhibit that I previously put on, the document that was signed by the three individuals, is a document that is important in both cases that are pending before this institution and historically. Now, what did Mr. Deronjic have to say about that document? He was the man who conceived of the document. He was the man who with the encouragement of Radovan Karadzic prepared it and had it executed. He said, and this is important, he said, "there is no true intention for the Muslims to stay in Srebrenica." He said it was prepared for propaganda reasons, and that its contents did not correspond with the truth. He said that the purpose for obtaining that document was to mislead the international community. Now, the information that he provided to us, debunking the contents of that document, is important for two reasons: It's important to diffuse any suggestion in trials that are ongoing or will be coming up in the future about Srebrenica that the Bosnian Muslims left the enclave because of their own free will. And two, it's important to negate the arguments of future revisionists that might use this document for the proposition that the forcible displacement of the Bosniaks from Srebrenica was a mere humanitarian evacuation conducted in accordance with the principles of international law. Such insinuations, I am quite sure, will continue to be made, and the only way to combat them is through the truth. And Mr. Deronjic has made a contribution to the truth in respect of that element of Srebrenica. Now, Your Honours, let me turn to a different area in which Mr. Deronjic has contributed to the Office of the Prosecutor. He has testified in four cases to date. The Prosecutor versus Krstic, was a Court witness in the appeals. The Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic as a Court witness. The Prosecutor versus Milosevic as a Prosecution witness, and I have already related to Your Honours the opinion of Mr. Nice and his assessment of Mr. Deronjic's testimony. And the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic as a Prosecution witness. He has also testified a fifth time before Your Honours yesterday and answered your questions about events leading up to and including the events at Glogova. Mr. Deronjic has been identified as a Prosecution witness in the case of the Prosecutor versus Krajisnik. It is my intention, with the Court's permission, to file with this Trial Chamber a transcript of his testimony in those proceedings as well as an assessment. Mr. Deronjic has also agreed to testify in other cases pending before this Tribunal as well as cases where persons who are not yet physically before the Tribunal, who are fugitives and who I am confident will someday arrive here, Mr. Deronjic has agreed to testify in certain of those cases. Those cases I have identified for Your Honours in a confidential memo previously filed with Your Honours. Mr. Deronjic has agreed to be interviewed and cooperate with OTP investigators in respect of other matters that are under investigation. Now, let me turn to another form of assistance from Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Deronjic has provided the Office of the Prosecutor with important original documentation in the form of minutes of meetings that took place in Bratunac in the SDS from 1990 to 1995. And these documents, these volumes here, are important documents for among other reasons, they provide us with insight into the manner in which the crisis staff and the SDS in Bratunac implemented, for example, the variant A and variant B instructions, the manner in which the crisis staff operated in general. Now, in addition to these two volumes, Mr. Deronjic has provided us with four original documents. These documents relate to war commissions and the creation of war commissions. Some are signed by Radovan Karadzic. These are documents that will be used in evidence in other cases. Turning to another topic, Mr. Deronjic has provided the Office of the Prosecutor with specifics about a crime that was committed in Bratunac in 1992; specifically, the arrest of Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica in Montenegro. He has identified people associated with that. Turning to another topic, Mr. Deronjic has provided us with the identities of perpetrators who were unknown to us. I won't go further on that. Now, as I said, Your Honours, at the beginning of my remarks, the case for which Mr. Deronjic has admitted his guilt is an extremely serious and grave crime for I would not hesitate to ask for the severest of sentences as I have done in the past in cases that I have prosecuted before this Tribunal. I've endeavoured to inform you and to inform the public of the reasons why I'm not making such a request in this case. Mr. Deronjic's early plea of guilt and principally, his very substantial and important cooperation with the Tribunal that I have detailed have led me and have led members of my Office to the conclusion that a different sentence is merited in this case. Therefore, Mr. President and Your Honours, for the reasons that I have stated today, I respectfully recommend that the Trial Chamber impose a sentence of ten years' imprisonment in this case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you. The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just one clarification. We conferred briefly on this issue, Mark Harmon, you made the point asking for leave to file additionally a statement and transcript in an upcoming hearing. The Trial Chamber believes that you have already provided sufficient material for the assessment of the contribution -- of the Prosecution that there is substantial contribution, and we should refer only to cases of the past and not in the future. And therefore, we regard it as not necessary to file this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be guided accordingly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, it's for the Defence, your concluding remarks, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, you have before you the accused, Miroslav Deronjic, who was arrested in front of his house in Bratunac on the 6th of July 2002 based on an indictment issued just three days prior to that, on the 3rd of July 2002, to be more precise. During his initial appearance before the International Tribunal on the 10th of July 2002, Mr. Deronjic pleaded not guilty to all events -- counts of the indictment. On the day between the 29th and the 30th of September 2003, the Prosecutor and Mr. Deronjic entered into a plea agreement according to which he agreed to plead guilty to one count of persecution, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(H), and 7(1), of the Statute of the Tribunal as described in the second amended indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. I'm awfully sorry. I don't want to normally to interrupt counsel, but for a better understanding, could you please explain what we have before us on the screen. I can read 1 September 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already indicated that this is something that we will tender, and I will explain what it is when we get to that point. This is the address of Miroslav Deronjic at a rally of the SDA. We talk about this yesterday. So when the time comes, we would like to play that clip. May I continue. Thank you. So in accordance to the agreement on -- the plea agreement, Mr. Deronjic understands that the Trial Chamber can bring a maximum sentence, a life sentence, in view of Miroslav Deronjic's full, substantial cooperation, the Prosecutor has recommended to the Trial Chamber the sentence of ten year imprisonment. No other promises or representations except those listed in the plea agreement were made by the Prosecutor in order to induce Mr. Deronjic to enter into a plea agreement. Based on factors and considerations described in Rule 101(B), the Defence has recommended to the Trial Chamber a sentence of not more than six years' imprisonment. On the 30th of September 2003, Mr. Deronjic entered a plea of guilty to the persecution charge in the second amended indictment. Having satisfied itself that the plea conformed with Rule 62 bis, the Trial Chamber accepted the plea of guilty. I would like to say something about the life of Mr. Deronjic. Miroslav Deronjic was born on the 6th of June in 1954 in the village of Magasici, the Municipality of Bratunac in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The village of Magasici before the war was inhabited mostly by Muslim citizens. Miroslav Deronjic's parents were a well-known and respected family. His father, Milovan, was a worker by profession, and his mother, Jelika, was a housewife. Mr. Deronjic has three sisters, Ljubica, Danica, and Dragica. Mr. Deronjic completed elementary school in Bratunac and secondary school in Srebrenica. Between 1973 and 1977, he attended the university of philosophy in Sarajevo majoring in history of literature of the Yugoslav peoples and the Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language. He majored in both above-mentioned sections with straight A grades, and graduated with honours with a bachelor of science degree in 1977. In the same year, he got a job with the Sarajevo daily newspaper Oslobodjenje. He also worked at Radio Sarajevo and for half a year as a teacher in the high school Igmanski Mars in Sarajevo. In 1979, Mr. Deronjic started working as a high school teacher in the high school in Srebrenica. In the period between 1983 to 1985, Mr. Deronjic worked in France as a teacher to children of Yugoslav workers employed abroad. When Mr. Deronjic returned from France, Mr. Deronjic became a language teacher in the Srebrenica high school where he worked until 1990. In 1984, Mr. Deronjic married Ranka Stevanovic from Bratunac. They have two sons, Neven, born in 1984, and Stefan, born in 1986. His wife tragically died in 1992, after which he married Danica Stevic in 1996. His second marriage produced two children, son Vuk born in 1996, and daughter Lola, born in 2001. Mr. Deronjic is father to four children, three of whom are minors. Your Honours, and now something about his political career. Mr. Deronjic joined the Serbian Democratic Party in 1990. Until that time, Mr. Deronjic had never been involved in politics and played no part in the creation of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Deronjic's political views were and remain anti-communist and democratic. And initially, he supported the Serbian Renewal Movement, the SPO, an opposition party in Serbia which vigorously opposed the regime of Slobodan Milosevic. Mr. Deronjic subsequently became the president of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bratunac in 1991, to be exact, and held that position until 1995. In 1993, he became a member of the main board of the SDS. After the signing of the Dayton Accords in 1996, Miroslav Deronjic became the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party. In April 1992, Miroslav Deronjic was elected president of the crisis staff of Bratunac and held that position until June 1992 when he withdrew from all functions within the community, political and civilian functions. Following after the tragic death of his wife, he temporarily withdrew from political life and devoted himself to his children. He withdrew from politics altogether in 1997. And from 1997 until the time of his arrest, he was unemployed. And now about his character, Your Honours. In the community in which he lived and worked amongst his colleagues, teachers, amongst pupils, in intellectual circles and in his private life, he was considered to be a clever, communicative person, tolerant in all respects, deeply committed to the subject that he taught to his students, and very much appreciating books, he was at the head of the library, and he transferred this love of books to all generations. Without any fee, as an extracurricular activity, he lectured his students in the history of art, transferring to them his affinity for art. The society in which he moved was a multiethnic one starting from his best man and maid of honour from his first marriage to his most intimate, closest friends. No one, could ever notice any aggression, hatred, or discrimination from Miroslav Deronjic on any grounds. Quite the contrary, he was graced with very positive human characteristics. Your Honours, with our final submissions, we submitted evidence of the personality and character of the accused from his friends, students, other intellectuals. And you can see that we are talking about representatives from all ethnic groups, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs who have given their contributions. The personality and character of the accused is also augmented upon by the expert psychologist Ana Najman in her written report and findings, describing Miroslav Deronjic as a person of above-average intellectual abilities from a group of those superior, and she did not notice any character traits such as discrimination, aggressiveness, or hatred with him. I would also like to say something about his struggle for democracy and his anti-communist feelings. At the time of one-party political order in the socialist society, Miroslav Deronjic was apolitical. All those who know him agree in one thing, that he had paid a very high price for his exceptionally anti-communist stance. With the beginnings of a multiparty political order, he began to get interested in politics because at the time he saw an opportunity to promote his anti-communist and democratic views. In that sense, he welcomed any political organising that had the same or similar goals. At the founding convention of the Party for Democratic Action which gathered and politically organised the Muslim population, Miroslav Deronjic also addressed those present on September 1st, 1990, at the stadium in Bratunac on behalf of the initiating committee for forming the Serbian Democratic Party, which had not been formed at that time. After some local Muslims leaders warmed up the atmosphere with nationalistically toned speeches, Miroslav Deronjic addressed also those present. He was welcomed with loud boos. However, after he welcomed the political rally of the Muslim population, and after he linked that with the anti-communist struggle and the spread of democracy, his address was followed by applause. Your Honours, with our final submissions, the Defence has attached the speech of Miroslav Deronjic of September 1st, 1990, at the founding assembly of the SDA in Bratunac. And with this submission now, we would like to also submit the video footage from that rally, and that is Document DS13/11. And the videoclip will also receive a marking A. I would like the technicians to play this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "Speaker: Thank you very much. I would now like to invite Mr. Miroslav Deronjic on behalf of the initiative board of the SDS. "Miroslav Deronjic: Respected people, distinguished guests, it is my honour to greet you. It is my honour to greet you on behalf of the Serb people of the Bratunac municipality, on behalf of the initiative board of the Serb Democratic Party of Bratunac, and on my personal behalf. Allow me to greet you with an old people's greeting: Peace, unity, and love amongst us brothers. "Being convinced that these words will dominate not only during today's gathering but in all other gatherings that we and you will organise in the future, as an expression of goodwill of both peoples in these times of political transformation, let reason and human dignity prevail. I am convinced that democracy is the only destiny of the Serbian people, as well as I'm convinced that democracy is the destiny of your people and all other people. Hatred, savagery, and primitivism have no chance in the world. Everyone who builds his policies on those principles is taking a huge responsibility for the destiny of their people. Who will be pushed to the margins of history, civilisation, and progress? Our joint fight must be aimed at opening up new spaces, spaces of culture, human relation, tolerance, and understanding, or as Mr. Crnjanski [phoen] said, that space of cheeriness in each heart and each mind. The one who succeeds in those endeavours will sooner bring his people into the family of happy European people. "Being convinced that our and your intentions are noble and being strongly convinced that you will persevere in them, allow me to welcome you again with yet another greeting. Let the party you are going to get today be happy, and long-lasting."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the clip, Your Honour. We have submitted two CDs in evidence which contain the entire footage of that rally with speeches of the Muslim leaders in order to corroborate our claim that in a very heated atmosphere created by them, Miroslav Deronjic gave a very tolerant, cultured speech to the Muslim population after which, as you saw, he was awarded with applause. The second reason why we wanted to tender this exhibit is that just like at that meeting, in no sentence did he invite or incite discrimination or hatred. Miroslav Deronjic in the same way in any of his public speeches, no matter whom he was addressing, Muslims or Serbs, at no meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party or earlier in his life as a teacher, as an intellectual, as a private person amongst his closest friends, he never referred to hatred and he never exhibited any discriminatory intent. And I have already submitted exhibits to corroborate this. I would like to say something about the war. From Croatia, the war spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina, aggravating interethnic relations. Miroslav Deronjic, in cooperation with Muslim representatives in the local authorities, attempted to find solutions so that ethnic tensions should not escalate into open conflict. An attempt to divide local power was carried out legally at a meeting of the municipal assembly in Bratunac and was implemented only as far as the division of the police is concerned. Miroslav Deronjic explained his reasons why this was not possible in the other spheres. For comparison's sake, that meeting of the municipal assembly was held on the 4th of April 1992 when war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Deronjic yesterday mentioned Zvornik and Bijeljina which were in immediately -- in the immediate vicinity. Perhaps it was possible to avoid open conflict had paramilitary volunteer units not appeared in the streets of Bratunac on the 17th of April 1992. From the very beginning, Miroslav Deronjic was the target of attacks by extremist members of these units because he did not welcome their arrival, and he publicly condemned their conduct. For them, Miroslav Deronjic was not a Serb, or he was "soft" as a Serb. And as far as the Muslim population was concerned and the membership of the SDS, he was an extremist Serb. It was not easy for him to find a formula of behaviour which would satisfy both sides. Fear, panic, collective frustrations, first killings, the eruption of open war in Srebrenica additionally aggravated the situation in Bratunac. And something now about Glogova. The village of Glogova is the largest village in the Municipality of Bratunac. And before the war, it was mostly populated by ethnic Muslims. It is on the main road between the town of Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. The village of Glogova separates Bratunac from the enclave of the Serbian village of Kravica. And the road which was the only link between Bratunac with the rest of the Republika Srpska passes through Glogova. During the war, all attempts by Muslim forces from Srebrenica to take Bratunac were made precisely through the village of Glogova by cutting Bratunac off from the territory under the control of Serbs. Precisely because of its importance, the village of Glogova during the war was often the target of operations and counteroperations of Muslim and Serbian military units. The way the village looked ultimately, completely torched and demolished, is actually the outcome of all of those actions and not only of the action carried out on the 9th of May 1992. In the afternoon of the 8th of May 1992, Goran Zekic, a well-known and popular political figure in Bratunac, who was a member of the Bosnian Serb Republic Assembly from the adjacent Municipality of Srebrenica, was killed near Srebrenica. And his body was brought to Bratunac. Srebrenica was from that day on under the control of Muslim forces. And in the course of that day and night, all Serbs left Srebrenica and fled either to Bratunac or to Serbia. Later the same day, at 2200 hours, the Bratunac Crisis Staff met, principally relating to the events surrounding the death of Goran Zekic and with the operation to attack Glogova. Miroslav Deronjic presided over this meeting. That meeting of the crisis staff -- at that meeting of the crisis staff, Miroslav Deronjic explained the strategic significance of the takeover of Glogova. He said that if the village did not put up any resistance, it is necessary that all Muslim citizens of Glogova be brought to the centre of the village and be transported in buses and trucks outside of the Bratunac Municipality, to Kladanj. He stated that the action of the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims, if the operation in Glogova should proceed well, should be continued over the coming days in the town of Bratunac itself and the local communities of Voljavica and Suha. Miroslav Deronjic also said that although it was not possible to foresee the events in Glogova, some houses should be torched as a warning to the Muslims. Miroslav Deronjic took part in the military operation against the village of Glogova as a member of the Territorial Defence, occupying with the unit to which he belonged an elevation above Glogova. In the morning hours, Miroslav Deronjic passed through Glogova intending to go to the funeral of Goran Zekic, who was killed. The funeral was to take part on that day. Yesterday, in the capacity of witness he said that while he was passing through there, he did not see any killed persons, and the mosque was not demolished. However, the Bosnian Muslim residents of the village put up no resistance. During the attack on the village, members of the attacking forces murdered 65 unarmed residents of the village. Miroslav Deronjic was not present during any of the killings, nor did he know about them on that day. After this action, actions with the same objective were carried out in the local communes of Suha and Voljavica, without the use of weapons and without burning of houses. The inhabitants of the hamlet of Mocilo, belonging to the village of Magasici, the closest neighbours of Miroslav Deronjic, Miroslav Deronjic, after that action, personally helped them to evacuate together with the Muslim population. Explaining his reasons for this, the witness, whose statement the Defence has tendered as an exhibit, says, paraphrasing the words of Miroslav Deronjic, "that was because an unfamiliar army arrived in Bratunac over which Miroslav Deronjic had no control. So out of fear for something bad to happen, he suggested that we temporarily leave the place and move either to Tuzla or Srebrenica. He then promised buses and an escort if the people opted to go to Tuzla. However, the people crossed over to the territory of Srebrenica in an organised manner. As that witness said, "Over those few days, no army members came to our village." People were not brought in. There were no abuses, nor killings, and no houses were burned. This happened between the 12th and the 13th of May 1992, so after the attack on Glogova. After the action against Glogova, Miroslav Deronjic at a meeting of the crisis staff proposed that a decision be adopted on the expulsion of the volunteers, which prompted some heated reactions amongst the part of the population which, in demonstrations the following day, also physically attacked Miroslav Deronjic and some members of the crisis staff. Representatives of the volunteer paramilitary formations beat up Miroslav Deronjic, and they also took him to the River Drina in order to execute him. In the warehouses called the hangar following this action, the volunteers held several hundred Muslim civilians. There was abuse there that was taking place as well as individual killings. Miroslav Deronjic initiated the adoption of a decision by the crisis staff to urgently during the night evacuate the civilians to Pale from where they were later exchanged. Yesterday, as a witness, Miroslav Deronjic talked about this exchange. This decision was another one in a series of clashes of Miroslav Deronjic with extremist forces which kept Bratunac under control. I would now like to say something about the criminal responsibility of Miroslav Deronjic in general. Yes, Miroslav Deronjic is guilty. He is responsible because he knew that the attack on Glogova and the forcible displacement of the Bosnian Muslim population from that village constitutes a part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian Bosnian Muslim population in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were declared as Republika Srpska. The decision to attack Glogova and to permanently displace its Muslim population was adopted with the objective of carrying out a plan for the creation of Serb ethnic territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Miroslav Deronjic accepted the concept of the creation of Republika Srpska, which was publicly promoted. But later, he also accepted a part of the plan for the creation of Republika Srpska which implied violent methods also in the form of the forcible expulsion of the Muslim population. Miroslav Deronjic is guilty because at the time when he ordered the attack on Glogova to be carried out, in view of the objective and purpose of the attack, the existing political climate, those units which would take part in the attack he could have foreseen and was prepared for that risk, that innocent Muslim citizens of Glogova could be killed, since this was a natural and foreseeable consequence. Miroslav Deronjic is aware of his part in this incident and his responsibility, and he sincerely admits his guilt, as well as expressing remorse and sympathy for the victims. With these broader submissions, the Defence wishes to indicate the reduced gravity of the act which the accused committed, and the reduced degree of his criminal responsibility in view of the temporal and territorial limitations of the acts of the accused, his prior conduct, his conduct following the critical events, as well as the circumstances in his immediate environment which had an unfavourable effect on the events in Bratunac. As far as the legal component of his responsibility, the Defence would like to present its views on that a little later. And now, Your Honours, I would like to say something about the applicable law on sentencing and the relevant practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia. But I believe that some other points from our address are more important. Articles 24(1) and Rule 101(B) provide that inter alia, the Trial Chamber, while determining a sentence, will take into account the sentencing practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia in their deliberations. The Trial Chamber is not obliged to stick to the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia while determining a sentence. However, it is obliged to take into account this practice as a source and as a form of assistance while determining the proper sentence. Article 41(1) of the criminal law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia provides for the following: All circumstances which influence the length of the sentence would be taken into account, such as mitigating and aggravating circumstances; and particularly, the degree of criminal responsibility; the motives for which the crime was committed; prior conduct of the perpetrator; his personal circumstances; and conduct following the commission of the criminal act; as well as other circumstances relating to the personality of the perpetrator. Article 42(2) of the criminal law of the Socialist Federal Republic Of Yugoslavia provides that the Judge may determine whether mitigating circumstances exist which are of such a nature that they indicate that the object of the verdict or the punishment can be equally met with a milder sentence. These provisions of the criminal law of the SFRY are similar to articles on sentencing policy provided in Article 24(2) of the Statute which instruct a Trial Chamber to take into account the gravity of the crime, as well as the personal circumstances of the convicted person. And Rule 101(B) which instruct the Trial Chamber to take into account all the aggravating and mitigating circumstances. According to Rule 101(A), a person pronounced guilty may be sentenced to a life sentence, or to a prison sentence including a life sentence. However, in view of the sentence that we are -- as Defence are suggesting to the Trial Chamber, the Defence believes that considering maximum sentences which could be pronounced for this crime or could be pronounced for similar crimes in the former Yugoslavia would not be appropriate at this time, and it would not be appropriate for the Defence to go into that. We will now speak about factors to be considered in sentencing and the objective of punishment. In the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the objective of punishment has three purposes: Retribution, interpreted as punishment of an offender for his specific criminal conduct; general deterrence, the prevention of future crimes; and rehabilitation. There are numerous judgements of this Tribunal which speak of these factors. In order to achieve the objective of the sentence, when determining a sentence, the following factors should be taken into account: The general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia, the gravity of the crime, and the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the commission of the crime, any aggravating circumstances, and any mitigating circumstances. Aggravating circumstances must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Mitigating circumstances need only be proved on the balance of probabilities. They need not be proved beyond reasonable doubt. In the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the following factors have been considered and accepted as mitigating factors: Admission of guilt; cooperation with the Prosecutor; remorse; voluntary surrender; good character; behaviour in the Detention Unit; and personal and family circumstances. In the Defence sentencing brief of the 18th of December 2003, we have referred to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal with respect to the factors that influence sentencing. I'm primarily referring to Celebici, Banovic, and Aleksovski. In the view of the Defence, the greatest wisdom is to determine the appropriate sentence in order to meet all the three component factors constituting the objective of the sentence. The penalty must be individualised and must result from consideration of all the facts and factors to be taken into account when determining the sentence. There is no doubt, and this is the practice adopted and a practice that the Defence accepts, the gravity of the crime and the form and degree of the participation of the perpetrator in the commission of the crime are fundamental in determining the sentence. And it is this I wish to say something about now; that is, the gravity of the crime and Miroslav Deronjic's form and degree of participation. The crime of persecutions from Article 5 of the Statute is in itself an extremely serious crime because it includes discriminatory intent, and it may be perpetrated in various ways and with various degrees of gravity, and also with varying forms and degrees of participation of the accused. The Defence is familiar with the standpoint that the act of persecutions may be committed only with intent as a form of culpability. For example, this standpoint is seen in the Stakic case and elsewhere. However, this form of culpability also has a more and less grave form. There is dolus directus and there is also dolus eventualis. The form and degree of the participation of the accused Miroslav Deronjic in the commission of the crime indicates that the milder form, dolus eventualis should be considered here. As described in the second amended indictment and the factual basis for the guilty plea, the accused committed the crime with the less grave form of intent; that is, dolus eventualis. The Defence wishes to observe that the degree of intent of the accused in relation to the most serious consequence which is reflected in the death of 65 civilians is closer to conscious negligence; that is, that in our view, it is at the lower end of the scale of dolus eventualis. I now wish to say something about aggravating circumstances. The Defence finds no aggravating circumstances in the case of the accused Miroslav Deronjic. All the aggravating circumstances of this crime, as well as those indicated in the Prosecutor's brief, are already subsumed in the offence of persecutions, and a part of the factual basis of the crime specifically committed by the accused. Or, according to the Tribunal's jurisprudence, they cannot be seen as separate aggravating circumstances unless they have been acquired in a specific criminal act and form part of the description of that act. Your Honour, I will now speak about the mitigating circumstances. The Defence finds that in the case of the accused, Miroslav Deronjic, all the mitigating circumstances are found which have been taken into account in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in sentencing. Not a single mitigating factor is lacking. In the view of the Defence, these are mitigating circumstances which indicate that the objective of punishment can be equally well achieved by a milder sentence. Let us begin with the admission of guilt. An admission of guilt demonstrates honesty and is important for the Tribunal in order to encourage people to tell the truth. An admission of guilt contributes to the fundamental mission of the Tribunal in establishing the truth with regard to the crimes falling within its jurisdiction. An admission of guilt is a unique and undisputed fact-finding tool which contributes to a large extent to peace-building and reconciliation among the warring communities. Individual responsibility, which leads to a restoration of the rule of law, reconciliation, and the restoration of peace on the territory of the former Yugoslavia is an integral part of the mission of this Tribunal. An admission of guilt contributes to the common good of the work of the International Tribunal by saving significant resources for the costs of investigations, fees for Defence counsel, and other costs of trials. An admission of guilt spares the victims and witnesses the stress of testifying. An accused who admits his guilt before the start of trial will usually be given full credit for his admission. Your Honour, these were just quotes from the various judgements of the International Tribunal which see the admission of guilt as a mitigating circumstance. In this specific case, Mr. Deronjic's admission of guilt demonstrates his sincerity and acceptance of responsibility for the criminal offences committed in Glogova on the 9th of May 1992. His acceptance of responsibility for these crimes and his personal responsibility will contribute to rendering justice for the victims, to deterring others from committing similar crimes, and will provide the basis for reconciliation in a very sensitive area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His admission of guilt, at least a year before the start of trial, is a significant contribution to the public significance of the International Tribunal. Your Honours, during its preparations and after the admission of guilt by the accused, interviewed how this act of his has influenced the victims. We have contacted victims from the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica, some of whom know Miroslav Deronjic personally. We have contacted persons who in this war which is fortunately behind us have lost their nearest and dearest, their fathers, brothers, sisters. There are some who have lost dozens of members of their extended families. However, some of them are already thinking in the following way: One of them says "I will not go into Miroslav Deronjic's guilt because I know nothing about it. I know that he has admitted guilt before The Hague Tribunal. To me personally, as a victim of the past war, this admission means a lot." There is another victim who also suffered grievously and who said: "In spite of everything, I think that all the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina have to turn a new leaf and turn to the future. It is only in this way there can be interethnic reconciliation. A contribution to this reconciliation can be made by the accuseds in The Hague regardless of what ethnic group they belong to by sincere remorse and admission of guilt." Your Honour, the Defence could have taken more similar statements; however, we have not tendered into evidence any of them, as you will have already observed. We felt that the position of the victims of the war is far more authentic when it is expressed through various organisations, associations, NGOs, and so on. The Defence notes that similar standpoints have been put forward by victims from the ranks of all three ethnic groups organised in associations such as the following: Women War Victims; Women of Srebrenica; Association of Former Camp Inmates, these are Croats; Association of Former Camp Inmates of Republika Srpska; and the Association Of Former Camp Inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the Association of Victims of Bosnian Ethnicity. At a conference on admission of guilt before The Hague Tribunal and the influence of an admission of guilt on the victims which was held in Sarajevo on the 5th and 6th of December 2003, and which was organised by the Sarajevo Human Rights Centre and the outreach programme of the Registry of the Hague Tribunal, the common standpoint of all the participants, which was the dominant viewpoint, may be summed up as follows: What is most important is to prove that a crime was committed, and therefore to unmask the policy on any of the three sides which led to this crime. In this sense, a sentence is a relative category because, Your Honours, there is no sentence that can give the victims full satisfaction for their losses. More detailed standpoints from the victims from this conference can be found in the Registry of this Tribunal. Therefore, what the victims of the war wish is something that Miroslav Deronjic has contributed to by his sincere and timely admission of guilt as an accused, and not only as an accused but also as a war victim. In the past war, and in connection with the war, Mr. Deronjic lost two brothers-in-law, his sister's husband and his first cousin's husband; he lost his wife; and 20 members of his immediate and extended family. His native village of Magasici was burned down twice. His family house burned down. The graveyard where his family was buried was destroyed, including his mother's grave and tombstone. Since 1992, two of his sisters have been refugees. There have been three attempts on his life by Serbs. He has been framed for murder. And the Belgrade press has accused him of treason. Your Honours, I now wish to say something about remorse as a mitigating circumstance. Remorse is a mitigating circumstance if the Trial Chamber is satisfied with the sincerity demonstrated. In the Banovic case the Trial Chamber took the position: "The Trial Chamber is, therefore, satisfied that the statements of the accused, both during the interview with the Prosecutor and at the sentencing hearing, are an expression of sincere remorse." In the course of years, Mr. Deronjic was interviewed countless times by the Prosecution. During these interviews, among other things, he expressed his deepest remorse. The Defence has provided the quotations from these interviews in its sentencing brief. We shall add that in the view of the Defence, remorse must be a real act. If remorse is only stated, declared, this cannot be a mitigating circumstance. Therefore, the very act of admission of guilt is the result of sincere remorse. Cooperation with the Prosecution and the endeavour to discover crimes and perpetrators is also a real indication of remorse. The accused will make use of the opportunity to express his remorse in public before Your Honours. As his Defence counsel, bearing in mind what I have said, I wish to say that this will only be the finale of years-long behaviour by the accused. Let me say a few words about voluntary surrender as a mitigating circumstance. The Trial Chamber in its judgement of Momir Nikolic found, I quote: "The Trial Chamber recognising the fact that Momir Nikolic did not evade the investigators cannot make the finding that had he known of his impending arrest, Nikolic would have surrendered voluntarily. In order to do so, the Trial Chamber would have to engage in speculation." Without going into the correctness of this standpoint, in the specific case of Miroslav Deronjic, this Trial Chamber need not speculate. During his meetings with the investigators, Mr. Deronjic explicitly stated his intention to surrender voluntarily, and this has been recorded in the transcripts of his interviews and the audiotapes. The indictment against Miroslav Deronjic was issued on the 3rd of July 2002. It was confirmed on the 4th of July 2002; and as soon as the 6th of July 2002, due to unusual expeditiousness on the part of the forces that arrested him, he was deprived of the opportunity to surrender voluntarily since at that time he did not know he had been indicted. In the Obrenovic case, the Trial Chamber found, I quote again: "The Trial Chamber finds his offer to voluntarily surrender, as reflected in the record of an interview held with the Prosecution, to be a factor in mitigation of the sentence." This standpoint is more than appropriate in the case of Miroslav Deronjic, and in the view of the Defence this circumstance in his case should also be taken as a mitigating circumstance. Now, I will say something about Miroslav Deronjic's substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor. Substantial cooperation is a mitigating circumstances in sentencing. Substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor is the only mitigating circumstances that is expressly mentioned in the Rules. An accused's substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor is the only mitigating circumstances which a Trial Chamber is obliged by the Rules to consider. In its sentencing brief, the Defence has quoted several judgements confirming these statements. The Defence has also tendered transcripts from the interviews given over many years of cooperation. Acting on orders from the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has submitted a confidential submission setting out the details of this cooperation. And today, we have heard about this cooperation in the exhaustive and extremely correct presentation by Mr. Harmon. Let me add only this: In his cooperation with the Prosecution, the accused has passed through all the stages of this process. He started as a potential witness, then he was a suspect, and finally an accused. After his arrival in The Hague, the accused continued his cooperation, and this resulted in an extensive interview and public testimony in very important trials which are underway, and he has also undertaken to testify in a number of trials which have not yet begun. In his wish to tell the truth, the accused invests all of himself and gives his all. He's sacrificing much. First of all, his family, which because of this had to enter a special protection programme. The Defence submits that the extent, quality, and sincerity of the accused's cooperation, it transcends anything yet seen before the Tribunal. The details, the number of facts, and the qualities of the evidence provided by Mr. Deronjic can also be seen from the Prosecution's written submission, the transcripts of his interviews, and his testimonies so far. The time period stretching from the prewar years to the end of the war, which are covered in his statements, the number of new facts, and the evidence previously unknown to the Prosecution that the accused has disclosed give this cooperation the highest value, even in the view of the Prosecution. The Statute, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal are not familiar with the institution of a crown witness. Comparative law is aware of this category from some legal systems and gives it great significance. Practically Miroslav Deronjic is a crown witness. In the view of the Defence, the Trial Chamber must view this cooperation as an especially mitigating circumstance. Your Honours, to conclude, I will say something about the personal and family circumstances of the accused as mitigating circumstances. In its introduction, the Defence has already said something about the personal and family circumstances of the accused. Until the time of the offence, Mr. Deronjic led an honest and honourable, respectable, private, professional and family social life. He had a distinguished career as a teacher of language and literature. He had no prior criminal behaviour or discriminatory behaviour, or criminal record of any kind, nor was he ever under any kind of investigation. He entered politics with the positive motives of anti-communist, democracy, and tolerance. He's a family man. His mother, Jelika, died in 1983. And his father, Milovan, who is now 80 years old, lives alone. After the tragic death of Mr. Deronjic's first wife Ranka in 1992, he was left alone with two sons, Neven, who was then aged 8, and Stefan, who was aged 6. He devoted himself entirely to his sons. He remarried in 1996 and has two children, Vuk and Lola, from the second marriage. Mr. Deronjic, therefore has four children, three of whom are minors. His wife and four children are in a witness protection programme as a direct consequence of his cooperation and guilty plea. The comportment of the convicted person while in detention and his general cooperation with the Trial Chamber and Prosecutor during the proceedings against him is also a mitigating factor. From the moment of Mr. Deronjic's arrest, he has always shown cooperation and respect for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor. While at the UN Detention Unit, Mr. Deronjic has fully complied with the terms and conditions imposed upon him. Let me now say something about the possibility of his rehabilitation. The process of rehabilitation of Mr. Deronjic began as early as 1997, when he had his first contacts with the Prosecution. This process is underway, and the time spent so far in the Detention Unit is producing results. If additional conditions are provided as suggested by the expert psychologist, Ms. Ana Najman, this process will be speeded up. And all this bearing in mind the positive character features of the accused. According to Rule 101(C), credit shall be given to the convicted person for the period, if any, during which the convicted person was detained in custody pending surrender to the Tribunal or pending trial or appeal. Mr. Deronjic was arrested on the 6th of July 2002, and transferred to the UN Detention Unit on the 8th of July 2002. He has remained at the Detention Unit from that date until today. And now, something about the sentence. The Defence has already pointed to the reduced gravity of the crime committed by the accused and the number of mitigating circumstances. Taking into account all this as well as his personality and character, in our view, retribution as one of the three purposes or components of the objective of punishment should not be given dominant -- a dominant role by the Trial Chamber. We submit that the objective of sentencing in the case of Mr. Deronjic will be achieved with a considerably milder sentence. Therefore, the Defence submits that a sentence of not more than six years would be appropriate for Mr. Deronjic, and that he should be given credit for time served in the Detention Unit. Your Honours, this is all I had to say, but I now ask Your Honours to give Mr. Miroslav Deronjic leave to address you personally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And DS18/8, also we will move the Trial Chamber to remove the seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's complete. So then time has come that we can hear the final word. Of course, it's only optional. Only Mr. Deronjic, in case you want to address the Trial Chamber, you will have now the right for a brief statement. And I think in the interests of all participants, we proceed for this about ten minutes instead of having a break. So if you could please be seated there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was born in a small place in Eastern Bosnia called Bratunac. I spent most of my life in that town. I grew up there, made my friends, and worked at the job that I was trained for. I established my family. I started my family. My life was no different from the life of the majority of the people I knew. In our neighbourhood, only about 10 kilometres away, there is a similar town called Srebrenica. We were connected by numerous connections which life itself weaved, business connection, family connections, neighbourly connections, kum connections. We lived our ordinary lives. Altogether, we were a little bit poor, a little bit forgotten by everyone. In the early 1990s, our common state began to break apart. The state was called Yugoslavia. Soon afterwards, war began. In the beginning, we hoped that perhaps it will not reach us. But connections amongst the people had began to break apart. Instead of our lives, the only true value that we had, we began to make up and accept some other values. Instead of ordinary words that we knew, we began to speak some great words: State, nation, religion. Those who taught us those words did not even know us, and we believed that they were doing that precisely for us. Soon, we understood that we began to be endless lines of dead in the chronicles of the dead, the missing, the bereaved. The war, which did not pass us by for some inexplicable reasons, expressed its anti-humane and anti-civilisational nature precisely there, all of its brutality, precisely in that area, its bloodiest and most terrible events were acted out. There is nothing that it did not touch. People, their property, everything that had been built up over decades, even the gifts of nature about which we were so proud, although we were poor, forests, places where we went for holidays. There is no way to explain and describe all of these things or express this entirely in words. When everything was over and it seemed as if it lasted for an eternity, those of us who survived, instead of the paradise that everybody promised, found ourselves in hell. Thousands of dead remained around us. Tens of thousands of destroyed homes. Deserted properties without people. Destroyed religious facilities. Bridges. Schools. Sadness and devastation remained inside us and all around us. Deep wounds which will continue to burn us for decades. Today, the town that I am speaking about, the town called Bratunac, is situated between two graveyards. One is on the northern side, and the other is on the southern side. One contains the bodies of one group, and the other contains the bodies of another group, divided even in death. Both graveyards came to be during and after the war. When you count all of those who are buried in those graveyards, there are twice as many of those than those who today inhabit that town. That is the result of war, the result of the terrible events we went through. That is the result of mindless political concepts to which we agreed and in which we participated. The town of Srebrenica does not exist any more. Whom does it belong to today? The Serbs? The Muslims? It is a town of the dead. Those who committed this killed a town. It doesn't have its present; it doesn't have its future. All that remains is its past which can be measured in centuries. Is there a greater condemnation for those who did that, no matter who they are and what their names are? They are hiding today, and they once spoke -- described themselves as heroes. They said that they were the faithful. How is it possible, then, that they're afraid of earthly justice and what are we to do with the justice that is expecting all of us quite soon? It is difficult to live with the memories of everything that happened, with the feeling of shame and embarrassment. In the years that are behind me, during many sleepless nights, I kept asking myself the same questions: How is it possible that we did this to each other? How is it possible at all that we agreed to something like this? If we are the way we are, is there anything salvation for all of us together? A lot of time has passed since then, and I haven't found the answers to those questions. But I know one thing: If the truth cannot save us, then really nothing can save us. And that is why, Your Honour, I spoke the truth. I'm not claiming that it is the only truth or the complete truth; the only thing that I am asserting is that I said everything that I knew, and that it is all correct. The truth may not be liked by everybody, but is it also necessary to say that I myself don't like it either? In numerous interviews to the Prosecution, which can be measured in thousands of pages, the four times that I testified before this Tribunal in different cases, I said everything that I had to say, including the truth about myself. From the very first day when I entered politics as far back as 1990 until the day I definitely left it, I did not conceal anything. I am what I am, no matter what that means. I cannot defend myself from myself. I accepted responsibility for Glogova, and I did not accuse anyone of the things that I am guilty of. I did not understand my guilt only in the legal sense, but in a broader, human sense. Even the things that I did not understand in the best way at the time or the things that I did not know, I was obliged to know and understand. Because I know, Your Honours, that I am capable of it. That is why my guilt is greater and more profound. I am aware of it completely, and that is why I admitted it. When I realised what really happened in Glogova, and I understood that for the first time completely when I was here listening to certain testimonies of survivors in other cases, I decided without much thinking to admit my guilt because what is my life in relation to the lives of those innocent victims? What is its value? And what can we measure it by? I did not calculate in any sense, particularly not in relation to a sentence which may be passed down. I did not think at that time, nor am I thinking about the sentence today. I have too many years and too much guilt to permit myself to think about that. I will accept my punishment in the same way that I accepted my guilt, aware that it cannot in any way be greater than the one I passed on myself, having permitted myself to be in the position that I am in and of which I am ashamed, aware that no punishment can pay my debts to the -- settle my debts to the living and the dead. I loved those towns in Eastern Bosnia. Today, they don't love me. They have renounced me, and that is my punishment. There is no greater punishment. Your Honours, I bow to the spirit of innocent victims in Glogova. Everything that I did in this Tribunal, for whatever it's worth, I dedicate to them in the hope that it will at least somewhat alleviate the pain of their dear ones. I am familiar with that pain because I also carry that pain. I regret the expulsion that I committed, and I express my remorse about all the victims of this war, no matter in which graveyards they lie. I apologise to all those whom -- to whom I caused sorrow and whom I let down. The last sentence that I wish to state before this Trial Chamber, I address exclusively, solely to my family, to my children: Never in this war did I wish, order, nor commit a single murder. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. You may be seated. Finally, I have to announce that the judgement in this case will be handed down after careful preparation in due course. We envisaged the 30th of March, Tuesday, the 30th of March, as the day for handing down the judgement, if the parties, please, can be prepared for this date that we can have the final hearing in this case. Any other additional remarks? I can see none. So therefore, the trial stays adjourned until further notice.
